Bartail flathead (Platycephalus westraliae) is a demersal species inhabiting the coastal waters of western and northern Australia, where it supports both commercial and recreational fisheries. Field studies have reported a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%] when water temperatures average 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This value is consistent with those observed in other platycephalid ambush predators, which typically exhibit relatively low reproductive allocations compared to more active benthic foragers. Such a strategy may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by a sit-and-wait predatory lifestyle on the continental shelf, where prey encounter rates are moderate. The available data suggest that reproductively active females allocate a limited fraction of their body reserves toward oogenesis rather than maintaining high fecundity, a pattern that often correlates with extended lifespans and iteroparous breeding schedules in teleosts of this ecological type.

Growth curve analyses based on otolith readings place the maximum or ultimate total length of this species at 55.3 centimeters [Li = 55.3 centimeters], a dimension that represents the asymptotic size approached by older individuals in unfished populations. This ultimate length is somewhat modest relative to other members of the Platycephalidae, several of which can exceed 70 centimeters, suggesting that P. westraliae occupies a middle range of somatic sizes within its genus. The associated asymptotic body mass, derived from length-weight regressions, has been estimated at 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams], reflecting a robust, laterally compressed body plan well suited for benthic ambush. Males and females appear to converge on similar asymptotic sizes, although females may exhibit slightly greater condition factors at equivalent lengths due to the energetic demands of oogenesis. These morphometric benchmarks provide useful reference points for stock assessment models, allowing fisheries managers to distinguish between growth overfishing and recruitment-driven changes in population structure.

Sexual maturation in Bartail flathead occurs at a total length of 29.6 centimeters [Lp = 29.6 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes. Reaching puberty at this intermediate body size allows individuals to embark on reproductive activity while still maintaining positive growth trajectories toward their asymptotic length. Field surveys of the gonadal condition of captured individuals indicate that by the time females attain this length, ovarian development has progressed to the vitellogenic stage, and males exhibit active spermatogenesis. The total length at puberty represents approximately 54 percent of the ultimate length, a ratio that aligns well with the broader patterns seen in iteroparous teleosts that mature at roughly half their maximum size. This relatively early maturation relative to ultimate size may be an adaptation to moderate natural mortality rates, ensuring that a sufficient proportion of the population reaches reproductive age before succumbing to predation or senescence.

Incubation experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] have documented that the egg hatching period or age at birth is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a brief embryonic duration consistent with the small pelagic eggs produced by this species. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae carry an initial wet weight at birth of roughly 0.00038 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00038 grams], an extremely small mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available before the onset of exogenous feeding. The larvae quickly progress through the lecithotrophic stage, with yolk absorption completing within the first 48 hours post-hatching, after which they must locate suitable zooplankton prey in the nearshore plankton community. This compressed developmental schedule at 22 °C reduces the window of vulnerability to planktonic predators, though it also demands that first-feeding larvae encounter adequate densities of copepod nauplii to avoid starvation mortality.

Estimates of maximum longevity for Bartail flathead, derived from tag-recapture programs and validated by otolith increment counts, place the lifespan at approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] under natural conditions at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This lifespan is moderate among Australian flatheads, some of which may exceed 12 years in cooler southern waters, reflecting the general correlation between environmental temperature and metabolic aging rates in fishes. Consequently, populations of P. westraliae may be sensitive to the removal of larger, older individuals, as these individuals contribute disproportionately to cumulative lifetime egg production and are likely the most experienced spawners in the population.
